newsitem.title: USA: IMF board to discuss Thai loan package on Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: IMF board to discuss Thai loan package on Wednesday.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's board will discuss a loan for Thailand on Wednesday, and Managing Director Michel Camdessus will hold a news conference the following day, an IMF press statement said.

"(Camdessus) will review the Thai economic package which forms the basis for Thailand's request for a standby credit which will be discussed on Wednesday, August 20, by the IMF's Executive Board," said the statement to correspondents.

The $4 billion IMF standby loan, if it is approved on Wednesday, will form a big part of a $16 billion international bailout to help ease a major cash crunch in Thailand, which was forced to devalue the baht currency in early July.

The loan is tied to a major economic reform package, including tighter fiscal and monetary policies and the publication of regular information on foreign reserves and central bank assets and liabilities.
The government on Tuesday approved plans to cut spending by 59 billion baht ($1.9 billion) in the 1997/97 financial year and create a budget surplus of 50 billion baht.

The loan package was agreed last week using fast-track rules drawn up by the IMF to cope with crises like that in Mexico in 1995. It is the largest loan since the Mexico crash, when the international community offered some $40 billion.

The United Stated played a key role in putting the Mexico package together, but Washington is not directly involved in the Thai package, where big loans are coming from Japan and other states in the region.
The baht devaluation had a knock-on effect across the south-east Asia region and other countries reluctantly abandoned the pegs which had held their currencies within broad ranges against the dollar.
Many currencies in the region are still under pressure, although economists admit that the countries do not share the economic problems behind Thailand's currency woes.

The Hong Kong dollar is the only regional currency still pegged to the U.S. dollar and the authorities, backed by their new Chinese masters, have said they are determined to defend their rigid monetary system. ((--Janet Guttsman, Washington newsroom, +1 202 898 8309))
